seo.title: Karmic tail 12 19 7 compatibility: waiting, light and the reins
seo.description: Karmic tail 12 19 7 compatibility: The Hanged Man, The Sun and The Chariot in a couple's matrix, what the three cards mean for two people and what to learn.

title: Karmic tail 12-19-7 in compatibility: the second half of Sleeping Beauty
short: In Charles Perrault's tale, Sleeping Beauty has no name. Aurora is the name of her daughter, and the daughter arrives only after the wedding, in the second half of the story, the half that later went missing. The couple karmic tail 12-19-7 tells the couple's story whole, second half included: first the waiting, then the light, and the main task begins exactly where storybooks write "and they lived happily ever after".

sections.h2: Why Sleeping Beauty is called Aurora
paragraphs: The version everyone knows was told by the Brothers Grimm in 1812. The prince passes through the briars, kisses the sleeper, she opens her eyes, the cooks and the flies in the palace wake up, there is a wedding, "and they lived happily together all their lives long". Tchaikovsky's ballet (1890) and Disney's film (1959) carry the story to the same wedding, and in both the princess is called Aurora.

Perrault's version, in his collection of 1697, often called the Tales of Mother Goose, is different. There is no kiss: the prince only kneels, and the princess wakes because, in Andrew Lang's English, "the enchantment was at an end". The wedding takes place that same evening, and it is the middle of the tale, not its end. Then the prince lives with his wife in secret for two years and tells his parents he is out hunting. They have two children: a daughter, l'Aurore, and a son, le Jour, Dawn and Day (Lang calls them Morning and Day). When the old king dies, the young one announces the marriage, brings his wife to the capital in state and soon leaves for a whole summer of war. He leaves the kingdom and his family in the care of his mother, and his mother is of the race of ogres.

It seems the daughter's name passed to the mother: everything after the wedding dropped out of the retellings, and all that survived of the second half was a name. In the Neapolitan Pentamerone of Giambattista Basile (1634–1636), where Perrault apparently found the plot, the sleeper's children are named even more plainly: Sun and Moon.

Tail 12-19-7 is the tale uncut. The Hanged Man is a hundred years of sleep and two years of secrecy, The Sun is two children named Dawn and Day, The Chariot is a campaign from which the king barely gets back in time. The part everyone knows is only the entry to the task. The task itself begins after the wedding.

sections.h2: Entry to the task: "You have kept me waiting a long time"
paragraphs: The first point of a couple's tail is what the two want together, their agreements and common language. It is something to lean on, but it stands on the line of tasks, and the same wish can turn into resistance. In this couple the shared wish is expressed by The Hanged Man, and The Hanged Man is life suspended in time.

Perrault's good fairy puts to sleep not just the princess but the whole castle: the maids of honour, the cooks, the beefeaters, the horses in the stables, the little dog on the bed. Even the spits full of partridges fall asleep, "and the fire as well" (et le feu aussi, in Perrault's French). The fairy makes sure the princess will not wake alone in a time not her own: the couple's world falls asleep and wakes together with her. Within a quarter of an hour a wood of trees and brambles grows round the castle, so that the princess "might have nothing to fear from any curious people". Before the prince the wood parts of itself and closes again behind him: none of his people can follow. This castle lets in only one.

A couple with The Hanged Man at the entry to the task recognises this castle: a world of their own where others do not go. The two have their own words and songs, their own jokes and habits, which look old-fashioned from outside. Helping his bride up, the prince notices she is "dressed like his great-grandmother" and tactfully says nothing; at supper the violins play "old tunes, but very excellent, though it was now above a hundred years since they had played". This is the beautiful side of the couple: the two know how to keep what the rest of the world has long since dropped.

In the original, the princess's first words are: "Est-ce vous, mon prince? Vous vous êtes bien fait attendre", that is, "Is it you, my prince? You have kept me waiting a long time." Turgenev, translating into Russian, made it otherwise: "Is it you, prince? And I have long been waiting for you!" (our translation from his Russian; Lang's English even turns it round, "You have waited a long while"). In Perrault it is a gentle reproach, in Turgenev a confession. The waiting is the same, but it is spoken in two different languages. A couple with this tail keeps coming back to this conversation: who waited for whom, for how long, and whether it was worth it. On good days it comes out as "I waited for you", on hard days as "you kept me waiting".

Perrault adds one more fine detail. The prince is more flustered than his bride, and the author explains why: she had had time to think what to say, for "it is very probable (though history mentions nothing of it) that the good Fairy, during so long a sleep, had given her very agreeable dreams". They "talked four hours together, and yet they said not half what they had to say". One of the two comes to the meeting with a ready-made script grown over years of waiting, the other comes with no script at all. A long wait leaves time to expect too much: Lisovskaya lists inflated expectations among the tasks of The Hanged Man in so many words.

In the second act the waiting turns from sweet to sticky. The morning after the wedding the prince returns to his father and says he lost his way while hunting and spent the night in "the cottage of a charcoal-burner, who gave him cheese and brown bread". For two years he goes "hunting" almost every day and never dares confess, because he is afraid of his mother. The decision is postponed until something outside makes it: the prince announces the marriage only when his father dies. Lisovskaya notes the same of a couple with this energy: such two come together slowly, and to get as far as marriage they often need a push from outside.

Today it looks like this. For years the two say "later": we'll move in later, tell the family later, decide later where to live. They are happy together, so "later" does no harm, until something external decides for them: a move, someone else's condition, an offer that cannot be refused. Perrault's prince assures his bride that he loves her "better than he did himself", and that too is the language of The Hanged Man: each is ready to set their own life aside for the other. At its best this is generosity; at its worst neither does anything for themselves and both wait for life to move them.

The main thing is visible already at the entry: in this union much is decided by the right time, not by effort. The princess wakes not from a kiss but because the hundred years are up, and even in Grimm the prince arrives on the very day they run out. That is the couple's gift, because the two can wait for their hour. It is also its risk, because one can wait for a deadline nobody has set.

sections.h2: Middle of the task: children named Dawn and Day
paragraphs: The middle of the tail is our reading of how the couple travels from its wish to its task, what it lives through on the way. For this couple the middle is The Sun, that is, a road through light.

In the tale the middle looks exactly like that. The secret marriage brings two children named after light: Dawn and Day, the son called Day "because he was a great deal handsomer and more beautiful than his sister". The secret comes out into the sun: the king announces his marriage, fetches his wife from the castle in the wood, and she enters the capital in full view, "riding between her two children". The couple that lived behind the briars becomes a couple the whole city watches. Lisovskaya's Sun paints exactly such a couple: bright, warm, noticed, talked about.

**The clue in the numbers.** The Sun is in neither partner's personal tail, in any couple of this kind. Tail 12-19-7 can be assembled from only three combinations of personal tails, and the nineteen in the middle is always the exact sum of the two personal middles: 9 + 10, 7 + 12 or 14 + 5. Neither of the two brings this Sun along. It is born between them, like Dawn and Day, who belong neither to the father nor to the mother alone.

There is a second clue. In almost half of these couples (48%) the two numbers that add up to The Sun are The Chariot and The Hanged Man, the very cards that stand at the two ends of the couple's tail. One partner has The Chariot in the middle of their personal tail, the other has The Hanged Man. Waiting and the road live in two different people, and the light appears only when the two are added together.

Sunlight has a property the tale mentions under its breath. By day everything is visible except what is whispered. "It was even whispered about the Court that she had Ogreish inclinations, and that, whenever she saw little children passing by, she had all the difficulty in the world to avoid falling upon them." The prince knew it, which is why he feared his mother. The Sun brought the marriage into the light, but the danger stayed a rumour: nobody said it out loud, and at the end "no one dared to tell" the king what was going on in his own courtyard. Among the minuses of The Sun in a couple's tasks, Lisovskaya lists not knowing how to talk about problems. For this couple the time of light is the best time to say out loud what the family usually whispers, before the campaign begins.

The second property of light is more treacherous. The brightest season looks like the ending. This is where the popular retellings cut the story: the grand entry, the children, the wedding feast, "happily ever after". In the middle of the tail it is easy for the couple to decide that everything has worked out, while the main task is still ahead.

sections.h2: Main task: war with the Emperor Cantalabutte
paragraphs: The main point of a couple's tail is read mostly through its minus: what does not work for the two and what they need to learn. For this couple the main task is The Chariot: movement, campaign, command, victory, the reins.

"Soon after the King went to make war with the Emperor Contalabutte, his neighbor." Perrault does not explain what the war is for. The neighbour has a comic name, the Emperor Cantalabutte (Lang spells it Contalabutte), and Turgenev turned him into "Tsar Kantalup", that is, a cantaloupe melon. The war lasts all summer, and in the tale it has no aim: it is a campaign that seems to happen by itself, because a Chariot is supposed to ride. Among the minuses of this energy Lisovskaya lists aimlessness, a contest over who leads, and the hard balance between work and family.

Before leaving, the king makes the tale's central mistake, and there is no malice in it. "He left the government of the kingdom to the Queen his mother, and earnestly recommended to her care his wife and children." The reins go to the one whose inclinations were only whispered about at court: she simply happened to be at hand. As soon as he is gone, the regent sends her daughter-in-law and the children to "a country house among the woods", back into the woods, to the beginning of the tale. Then she tells her clerk of the kitchen: "I have a mind to eat little Morning for my dinner to-morrow", with a sauce Robert.

What follows shows what becomes of a house without reins. The young queen is sure her children are dead, and when the clerk comes with a dagger she stretches out her own neck: "Do it; do it… Execute your orders." In the last scene the queen and her children, the clerk, his wife and their maid are brought into the courtyard, and the ogress has given orders that they come "with their hands tied behind them". Whoever was left at home without the reins goes back to the language of the entry: waits, sacrifices themselves, waits for the verdict and the rescuer.

The rescuer comes: "the King (who was not so soon expected) entered the court on horseback (for he came post)". This is The Chariot at its best: its speed and resolve at last working for the home. Only he arrives at the very edge of the tub of snakes.

In life the regent is rarely an ogress mother-in-law. Lisovskaya does list the power of parents over the couple among the minuses of The Hanged Man, but far more often the reins go elsewhere. It may be work that runs the house on its own timetable, tiredness or habit, the phone, relatives, or simply whoever is nearest. A couple with this tail recognises the scene: one sets off on their own summer campaign, a project, a business trip, a career leap or a building job, and tosses over a shoulder "keep an eye on things". The other stays and does not feel entitled to decide: holds the fort and waits for the return. After a while each pulls the blanket their own way, and the house lives a life of its own.

In the tale the roles are handed out the old way: he rides, she waits. In a couple with this tail the roles do not depend on sex. Either of the two may ride and either may wait, and most often they take turns.

The task is not never to leave. The Chariot has to move, and in Lisovskaya's plus of this energy each partner has a life and growth outside the family: walking side by side, each on their own road. The task is something else:

ul: to agree before the campaign, not after, who holds which reins and what gets decided without the one who is away;
not to make a hostage of the one who stays: whoever is at home governs, rather than waiting with tied hands;
to name the status of the relationship and the roles without evasion, since two years of secret marriage were exactly that evasion;
to come back regularly, and not only at the last minute, by post horses, to the very edge of the tub.

sections.h2: The circle of the tail: a tale that begins and ends with waiting
paragraphs: Put the first and last pictures of the tale side by side and the tail's mechanism shows. The first picture is a castle where people cannot move and wait for a rider. The last is a courtyard where people have their hands tied and are again waiting for a rider. Between them lie the light, the children, the grand entry. If the Chariot's task is not solved, the circle closes: waiting, light, campaign, and waiting again, only now not sweet but anxious.

The circle has a price. Years lived in "later". The one who waits grows used to being rescued. The one who rides grows used to coming back a hero at the last moment and does not notice that a regent ran the house all summer. And above all, the couple comes to believe that waiting is its moral.

Perrault's own moral also looks only at the entry. The verses after the tale speak only of the first half, as if there had been no ogress at all: "To wait a while for a husband, rich, well-made, gallant and gentle, is natural enough; but to wait a hundred years, and asleep the whole time, you will not find a woman now who would sleep so calmly." The tale, he goes on, seems to tell us too that the bonds of marriage, when delayed, are often no less happy, "and that one loses nothing by waiting". And at once he does not believe it himself: the fair sex longs for marriage with such ardour that he has "neither the strength nor the heart to preach this moral" to it (our translation). In French the line, on ne perd rien pour attendre, today also sounds like a threat, something like "just you wait". Once again this couple's waiting has two faces.
The moral of tail 12-19-7 is not "wait". The couple knows how to wait from the very entry. Its moral is to drive.

sections.h2: What Waite saw: a spinner, two children and a rider
paragraphs: In the first part of his book Waite describes how The Sun was drawn before him. On older cards there is "a wall suggesting an enclosure—as it might be, a walled garden—wherein are two children", running hand in hand. "Éliphas Lévi says that these are sometimes replaced by a spinner unwinding destinies, and otherwise by a much better symbol—a naked child mounted on a white horse and displaying a scarlet standard." Perrault's tale holds all three versions of the card. The spinner is the old woman at the top of the tower, "alone, spinning with her spindle", who "had never heard of the King's proclamation against spindles": the sleep begins with her. The two children are Dawn and Day. The rider is the king who rides into the courtyard and ends the tale, and a child with a weapon is there too: three-year-old Day, whom the clerk finds "with a little foil in his hand, with which he was fencing with a great monkey". One sentence of Waite's about the old Suns runs through the whole tale, from the tower to the courtyard.

In the same part Waite describes The Hanged Man as a figure "suspended head-downwards", and "the arms are bound behind him". The last scene of the tale divides these two features between its characters. The hands bound behind fall to the queen, the children, the clerk, his wife and the maid. Head down goes the ogress: seeing that all is discovered, she "threw herself head foremost into the tub". In Waite's divinatory list the reversed Hanged Man begins with the word "Selfishness". In the tale the ogress's appetite answers to it: someone else must be the sacrifice.

About The Chariot, Waite reports something curious. Court de Gébelin, the man who in the eighteenth century first declared the Tarot an Egyptian book, said "that it was Osiris Triumphing, the conquering sun in spring-time having vanquished the obstacles of winter". Waite disagrees, but for an eighteenth-century reader the last two cards of this tail were one light: The Sun, and the sun in a triumphal chariot. This is the danger of the middle: light easily turns into triumph, and triumph into a campaign. In Perrault there is a single sentence between the grand entry into the capital and the war.

In her account of The Chariot, Wen writes that "the castle walls and moat behind him represent the domain that he protects". The charioteer protects what lies behind his back, and faces the other way. The first chariot in the tale appears long before the king: the good fairy arrives to put the castle to sleep "in a fiery chariot drawn by dragons". A chariot brings sleep at the beginning; a rider ends the waiting at the end.

Wen has one more detail, the elements of the cards. For her, "the element of Water governs" both The Hanged Man and The Chariot, and in both "yin energy is dominant". The Sun is Fire, with yang dominant. Tail 12-19-7 comes out as water, fire and water again, and the only fire burns in the middle. In Perrault's castle, remember, even the fire in the hearth falls asleep for a hundred years.

sections.h2: How the couple's tail 12-19-7 is worked out
paragraphs: Each point of a couple's matrix is the sum of the same points of the two personal matrices, reduced to 22: if the sum is greater than 22, its digits are added together. The couple's tail is three points: the entry to the task, the middle and the main task.
An example is a couple with the dates of birth 06.03.1978 and 14.09.1975. The first partner's personal tail is 21-10-16, the second's is 18-9-9. Add them point by point:

Here the sum of the two end numbers also gives 19, because 12 + 7 = 19, but a couple's middle is not worked out that way: it is always the sum of the middles of the two personal tails. In the centre of this couple's matrix stands Temperance (5 + 9 = 14), and in the couple's values, The Lovers.
Tail 12-19-7 occurs in roughly one couple in 192 (0.522%) and ranks 53rd of the 97 couple tails. There are only three ways to assemble it:

There are no other couple tails made of the numbers 12, 19 and 7; this order is the only one. The same order also occurs as a personal karmic tail, for 4,296 birth dates since 1900, but that is a different calculation and the points play different roles. The personal tail 12-19-7 has its own article; this one is only about the couple.

sections.h2: Centre and values: an angel named Time
paragraphs: The centre of a couple's matrix is the atmosphere, what happens between the two when nobody is watching. In couples with tail 12-19-7 the centre is almost always Temperance: in 99.2% of them. The remaining 0.8% have The Hierophant.

Wen quotes P. D. Ouspensky, who called Temperance the Time card: "The name of the angel is Time.… One of the cups the angel holds is the past, the other is the future. The rainbow stream between the cups is the present. You see that it flows both ways." In Perrault time is literally poured from cup to cup. The young queen "was turned of twenty, not reckoning the hundred years she had been asleep", she wears her great-grandmother's dress, and a century-old music plays at supper. Inside such a couple past and future also flow both ways: old dreams pour into the present day, and plans pour back into memory. Lisovskaya's Temperance at its best means quarrels settled by talk and concession, and a balance of rest and movement. This, it seems, is the two people's skill at blending waiting and the road.

In Waite's divinatory list Temperance carries "Economy, moderation, frugality, management, accommodation". All summer the house is saved not by the king or the queen but by the clerk of the kitchen, Perrault's maître d'hôtel, the master of the table. In place of Dawn he serves a lamb, in place of Day a kid, in place of the queen a young hind. Perrault's verb is accommoder une biche, "to dress a hind", from the same root as Waite's accommodation. Temperance at the centre of the couple works like this clerk: quietly substitutes, softens, buys time. That saves the day while the king is away. But if it goes on too long, one partner ends up hiding the trouble in the kitchen instead of bringing it out into the courtyard.

The rare couples with The Hierophant at the centre have a key of their own, and Waite has it too. Among the reversed meanings of Temperance he lists "sometimes even the priest who will marry the Querent". In Perrault the lord almoner, who slept a hundred years along with everyone else, marries the couple right after supper, "without losing any time". For such couples the atmosphere rests on rule, on ritual, on "the way things are done".

The couple's values are what the union exists for. In 61.8% of couples with this tail this is The Lovers, that is, choice. Perrault's prince makes up his mind "sans balancer", "without weighing the matter", the moment the old countryman tells him of the sleeper. For these couples the value lies in choosing each other again, above all at the moment the campaign calls. In 38.2% the values hold The Devil. Lisovskaya's main thought about this energy in a couple is that nobody belongs to anybody. In the tale the ogress treats the house as her table, and the king leaves her his wife and children along with the kingdom, as if they were property. For these couples the value lies in holding the reins, not owning them.

sections.h2: The strong version: four hands on the reins
paragraphs: Tail 12-19-7 makes a couple neither happy nor unhappy. It shows the place where the plot usually breaks, and what mends it.

ul: **Waiting needs a term and a reason.** The fairy had a term, a hundred years. A pause with no term turns into a sleep after which everything in the castle is a century out of date. "We wait until spring, because…" is a decision; "some time later" is that very hedge of briars round the castle.
**In the light, name what is whispered.** The Sun is direct light. The time when the couple is happy and seen is the best time to say aloud what each of them fears, rather than leave it to rumour.
**Agree before the campaign.** Who decides what while one is away, whom the one left behind can lean on, what must not be handed to a "regent", be it work, relatives or habit.
**The one at home governs too.** This couple's Chariot is driven with four hands: one holds the reins of the road, the other the reins of the home, and next time they swap.

**Come back sooner than expected.** Perrault's king arrives earlier than he was expected, and only for that reason does everything end well. In the strong version of the tail this is not a miracle by post horses but a habit.

paragraphs: In the strong version the couple keeps the gift of its entry: the knack of waiting, the slow coming together, the old music only the two of them hear. It does not, however, mistake waiting for fate. It brings its light out into the day and says aloud what used to be whispered. And it drives together: one on the road, the other at home, then the other way round. Then the tale ends not with a tub of snakes but with the words of Perrault's moral, which at last come true: delayed bonds are no less happy.

intro: The three cards of the couple's tail stand in the same order as the three acts of the tale:

ul: **12 · The Hanged Man — entry to the task.** What joins the two is a shared language of waiting: "not yet", "let's wait", a life both are willing to keep on hold for each other's sake. It is how the couple begins, and it is also what holds the couple back.

**19 · The Sun — middle of the task.** The way runs through light: what was hidden comes out into the day, and the couple gains something everyone can see, a shared home, children or a shared venture, a joy that no longer needs hiding.

**7 · The Chariot — main task.** Learning to drive together: not handing the reins of the shared home to someone else when one or both are called away on campaign, and coming back before the last minute.

intro: The tail does not predict what will happen to the couple. It shows a plot in which two people recognise themselves, and the place where that plot tests them in earnest. For this tail, that place is not the meeting but the time after it.

faq.q: How is karmic tail 12-19-7 in compatibility worked out?
faq.a: Two dates of birth are needed. A personal matrix is built for each partner, then the points of the tail are added in pairs and reduced to 22: entry with entry, middle with middle, main task with main task. For example, 06.03.1978 and 14.09.1975 give the personal tails 21-10-16 and 18-9-9, and together 39 → 12, 19 and 25 → 7. The compatibility calculator on the site does this by itself.

faq.q: How does the couple tail 12-19-7 differ from the personal tail 12-19-7?
faq.a: The personal tail 12-19-7 is worked out from one date and describes one person, and its points have their own roles. The couple's tail is built from two personal matrices and describes the task of the union: the entry to it, the middle and the main task. The numbers are the same, but **the calculation and the meaning differ**, so readings of the personal tail do not carry over to the couple.

faq.q: Is tail 12-19-7 a bad sign for a couple?
faq.a: No. A couple's tail does not predict break-ups, wars or misfortunes, and it does not grade the couple. It shows what the two meet on (waiting), what they pass through (the light of an open shared life) and what they learn (to drive together). The minus of the main task is something to work on, not a verdict.

faq.q: Are there couple tails with the same numbers in another order?
faq.a: No. From the numbers 12, 19 and 7 a couple can only get the order 12-19-7: The Hanged Man at the entry, The Sun in the middle, The Chariot in the main task. No other arrangement occurs in a couple's matrix.

faq.q: What stands in the centre and in the values of a couple with tail 12-19-7?
faq.a: In the centre of the couple's matrix, 99.2% of such couples have Temperance and 0.8% have The Hierophant. In the couple's values, 61.8% have The Lovers and 38.2% have The Devil. Temperance in the centre is an atmosphere in which the two blend waiting and movement, past and future. The Lovers in the values mean choosing each other again, and The Devil teaches that nobody belongs to anybody.

report.h3: A castle that lets in only one

report: Perrault's fairy puts the whole castle to sleep: the maids of honour, the cooks, the horses in the stables, the little dog on the bed. Even the spits full of partridges fall asleep, "and the fire as well". A wood of brambles grows up in a quarter of an hour, parts before the prince and closes again behind him, so that none of his people can follow. The prince notices that his bride is "dressed like his great-grandmother" and tactfully says nothing, and at supper the violins play music that has not been heard for a hundred years.

The common language of such a pair is waiting. In Perrault the princess's first words are a gentle reproach: she has been kept waiting a long time. Turgenev turned them into a confession that she has long been waiting. The waiting is one, but it speaks two languages, and the couple keeps coming back to the same conversation: who waited for whom, and whether it was worth it. She had had time to think everything over while the fairy gave her agreeable dreams; he arrived flustered and without ready words. A long wait leaves time to expect too much.

Then the waiting turns sticky. For two years the prince goes "hunting", tells his father a story about a night in a charcoal-burner's cottage, and never dares confess to his mother. He brings himself to announce the marriage only when the old king dies. The decision waits for a push from outside, and that is the brake built into this entry: years lived in "later", and a deadline nobody has set.

report.h3: A light in which whispers go unheard

report: The middle of the tail is a road through light. The secret marriage comes out into the day: the king announces it, and his wife enters the capital in full view, riding between her two children. This couple's Sun is in neither partner's personal tail: **it is born only between the two of them**, like Dawn and Day.

But by day everything is visible except what is whispered. "It was even whispered about the Court that she had Ogreish inclinations." The Sun brought the marriage into the light, but the danger stayed a rumour, and at the end "no one dared to tell" the king what was going on in his own courtyard. The season of light is the best time to say aloud what the family usually whispers. There is a second trap too: the brightest season looks like the ending, and that is exactly where the popular retellings stop.

report.h3: A kingdom left to a regent

report: The main task is The Chariot. The king goes off for a whole summer of war with the Emperor Cantalabutte, and the tale never says what the war is for. He leaves the kingdom and his family to his mother, whose inclinations were only whispered about at court. There is no malice in it: the reins simply go to whoever is at hand. The regent sends her daughter-in-law and the children back into the woods, and the young queen, sure that her children are dead, stretches out her own neck: "Do it; do it." In the last scene the queen and her children are brought into the courtyard "with their hands tied behind them". **Without the Chariot's task solved, the couple returns to its entry:** waiting again, sacrificing again, waiting for a rescuer. The rescuer comes, "not so soon expected", on horseback, "for he came post", but he arrives at the very edge of the tub of snakes.

In life the regent is usually not a mother-in-law. It is work that runs the house on its own timetable, tiredness, habit, relatives. One partner sets off on a summer campaign of their own, a project, a business trip or a career leap, and tosses over a shoulder "keep an eye on things". The other stays and does not feel entitled to decide. In the tale he rides and she waits, but in a couple with this tail the roles do not depend on sex: either of the two may ride and either may wait, and more often they take turns.

report.h3: The moral is not to wait

report: Perrault's own moral speaks only of the first half: delayed bonds of marriage are often no less happy, and one loses nothing by waiting. Of the ogress, not a word. **The moral of tail 12-19-7 is not to wait but to drive together.** This couple knows how to wait from the very entry. The Chariot has to move, and each partner may have a road of their own, but the reins of the home are handed to no one. Simple things change the script:

ul: giving the waiting a term and a reason: "we wait until spring, because…" instead of "some time later";
in the light, saying aloud what each one fears;
agreeing before the campaign who holds which reins and what gets decided without the one who is away;
the one at home governs too, rather than waiting with tied hands;
coming back sooner than expected, and making it a habit, not a last-minute miracle.

report: In the strong version the couple keeps its gift: the slow coming together and the old music only the two of them hear. It does not, however, mistake waiting for fate. It brings its light out into the day and **drives with four hands on the reins**: one on the road, the other at home, then the other way round. Then the tale ends not with a tub of snakes but with Perrault's words, which at last come true.

unit.title: The second half of the tale

captions.M: A shared language of waiting, a world that lets in one
captions.N: A light born only between the two of you
captions.D: Drive together; never leave the home's reins to a regent

unit.meaning: Waiting comes to you naturally from the start; your task is to drive together and not leave home to a regent on campaign.
